source_lines.40: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this norm-completion construction, and let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Order its finite-dimensional complex subspaces by inclusion. This is a directed system because the span $F+G$ of any two finite-dimensional subspaces is finite-dimensional. To each such $F$, assign the finite-dimensional CAR C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-dimensional-car-algebra-is-matrix-algebra]], with the generator-preserving maps of [[lem-car-finite-subspace-inclusions-are-isometric]]. Identify each stage with its image under these injective maps and let $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ be their algebraic union.
source_lines.42: The common finite-stage norm is well defined on this union because every inclusion is isometric. Under Countable Choice, [[thm-metric-completion-exists]] supplies a metric completion and [[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]] equips it with the compatible Banach-space structure; this is the norm completion of [[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]. Define the **CAR C*-algebra over $H$**, $\mathsf{CAR}(H)$, to be this norm completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$. Addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and involution are the compatible finite-stage operations; submultiplicativity and isometry of the involution make them extend continuously to the completion, and the C*-identity passes to limits. The identity is nonzero because the zero-dimensional stage is $\mathbb C$ and every inclusion preserves its unit. For $f\in H$, write $c(f)$ for the image of the generator in the stage $\operatorname{span}\{f\}$; the universal inductive-limit property and its norm are proved in [[thm-general-car-has-universal-inductive-limit-norm]].

Regular isotopy is generated by planar isotopy and Reidemeister moves II and III. A positive curl is a one-crossing curl whose oriented self-crossing has sign $+1$; its sign is independent of the direction chosen on its component. There is a unique function $P$ from link diagrams, including the empty diagram, to $A$ with $P(\varnothing)=1$, unchanged by regular isotopy, satisfying the following local rules: a positive or negative curl multiplies $P$ by $a$ or $a^{-1}$; a disjoint trivial circle multiplies $P$ by $d$; and $P(L_+)-P(L_-)=s(P(L_0)-P(L_\infty))$. Here in an oriented disk with four cyclically labelled endpoints $1,2,3,4$, $L_+$ connects $1$ to $3$ over the strand from $2$ to $4$, and the two smoothings are chosen so that the oriented smoothing for any orientation making this crossing positive is $L_0$; $L_-$ reverses the crossing and $L_\infty$ is the other smoothing. Rotating the disk interchanges both differences and preserves the rule. In particular the empty diagram freely generates the quotient of the free $A$-module on closed diagrams by these rules.

source_lines.50: 4.1 The multi-component switch set for lifting a fixed component is independent of point and direction, so step 2.1 makes its expansion independent of these choices. For a knot, moving the point past one encounter with a crossing toggles exactly that crossing in the descending switch set. The two terminal descending diagrams differ by switching this crossing, which is the first or last encounter from the new point. Their terminal values satisfy the required sum-skein equation: if their writhes are $v+1,v-1$, the two smoothings have values $b^v$ and $hb^v$. To see this, the smoothing that separates the traversed initial portion produces two descending unknots with one over the other; the other is their connected sum with possibly one direction reversed. Their total self-writhe is $v$, since the mutual crossing-sign sum of the two separated portions is zero: one lies over the other, and their algebraic planar intersection number is zero. Both diagrams reduce by pulling these overlying arcs away, followed by removing curls, so their evaluations follow from lower-crossing invariance and curl factors. The equation is $b^{v+1}+b^{v-1}=t(1+h)b^v$. By commuting the toggled switch to the beginning of the expansion, this terminal equality makes $Q(D,p)$ unchanged. Moving the point around all arcs proves point independence. Averaging the two directions makes direction independence explicit. Agreement with the terminal scalar on descending diagrams is deferred until after regular-isotopy invariance; point independence alone does not identify the two directed expansions. source_lines.58: 8.1 For move III, label the three local arcs by their height order. First give them the height order in which they are first encountered in a chosen traversal or component-lift expansion. The six possible height orders are connected by exchanging adjacent heights. Such an exchange switches one corresponding crossing on both sides of the move. Apply the sum-skein equation at those crossings: each sum of the old and switched evaluations is $t$ times a pair of smoothing evaluations. The two pairs agree. One smoothing cancels the two remaining crossings by move II or identifies them by planar isotopy; the other slides a cup past them. Here is an endpoint description of the cup slide, independent of any BMW presentation. In the following diagram words the factors are stacked from top to bottom in their written left-to-right order. In a three-strand rectangle let $e_j$ denote the actual crossing-free cup and cap joining adjacent positions $j,j+1$, and $x_j$ the actual crossing at those positions. The diagrams $e_1x_2x_1$ and $x_2x_1e_2$ both reduce to the diagram with upper cup $(1,2)$, lower cap $(2',3')$, and an untwisted strand from $3$ to $1'$. Slide the arc attached to the cup across the two crossing disks; the two successive over/under encounters then bound a bigon and cancel by move II. Likewise $x_1x_2e_1$ and $e_2x_1x_2$ reduce to upper cup $(2,3)$, lower cap $(1',2')$, and the strand from $1$ to $3'$. These are identities of the smoothed diagrams by planar deformation and move II, concerning at most $N-1$ crossings, rather than assumed identities in an abstract algebra. Thus the equality of old evaluations is equivalent to equality of switched evaluations. The adjacent-height exchanges reach every type III configuration, proving move III invariance for every traversal, component choice and outside diagram. Consequently a descending knot $U$ now has $L(U)=b^{w(U)}$: pull its descending arc away by nonincreasing moves II and III until only curls remain, then use step 6.1.
